title: Summer learning works. So, why can’t more kids access it?
summary: Summer is a break for kids, but a challenge for families looking to keep them "fed, safe and engaged," and the "summer slide" threatens the state's educational goals. That's why Ellie Mitchell and Brodrick Clarke say we must push for accessible summer programming.
content:
by Ellie Mitchell and Brodrick Clarke, Maryland Matters July 16, 2026

by Ellie Mitchell and Brodrick Clarke, Maryland Matters July 16, 2026

Summer can be a magical time in a young person’s life. The daily burdens and stress of the school year lift, the days grow longer and sunnier, and in Maryland, the ubiquitous snowball stands reopen for the season.

Along with the freedom that summer provides comes a set of tensions that nearly every family faces. Where will the kids go? What will they do? How can we keep kids fed, safe and engaged?

Summer learning opportunities offer critical supports. When done right, summer programs are the places where kids discover hidden talents, open doors to new worlds, meet new friends, gain mentors, and build lasting memories.

Many young people rely on school meal programs for breakfast, lunch, and sometimes snacks and supper. When school is out, food insecurity rises. Beyond safety and supervision, summer programs keep kids mentally engaged, staving off the well-researched “summer slide.” If Maryland wants to meet its ambitious goals for literacy and math proficiency, we ignore summer at our own peril.

The need is urgent, and the gap is wide. According to the Afterschool Alliance’s America After 3 PM Summer Report, 218,095 Maryland children — two in five — whose parents want to enroll them in a summer program are missing out because programs are either unavailable or too expensive.

When COVID-19 recovery funding for public schools ended, we saw a steep decline in school-based summer programming. We also saw districts shift to half-day models to offset costs, sacrificing convenience for working families. That trend continues this summer.

The stakes are especially high for older youth. Gov. Wes Moore has called on the Department of Juvenile Services to develop a youth summer safety strategy, but that challenge grows steeper as safe gathering spaces for teens continue to shrink. This year’s outlook for summer youth employment is the worst in decades.

When young people gather and incidents occur, media coverage tends to spark hand-wringing about public safety without a corresponding push to expand opportunities for this age group. We can do better.

That’s why the Maryland Out-of-School Time Network has convened a group of leaders to take action through the Maryland Summer Learning and Achievement Task Force. MD-SALT will undertake a yearlong examination of summer programs across the state and make concrete recommendations to Maryland policymakers on expanding access to these critical supports.

Recommendations are already emerging. We need better data to understand where the gaps are most acute. We need expanded public and private investment to increase the number of affordable summer seats statewide. And we need stronger partnerships between communities and schools to offer a wide variety of engaging, age-appropriate programs for students from pre-K through 12th grade.

There is good news in the Afterschool Alliance report: Investing public dollars in summer learning is broadly supported across political affiliations. Families who can access summer experiences for their children overwhelmingly give them high marks. We celebrated National Summer Learning Week July 6-10 to highlight innovative and high-quality programs around the state.

The path forward requires public will at the local and state levels, alongside private and philanthropic investment. One opportunity is to direct future Social Media Lawsuit settlements into resources for high-quality In-Real-Life experiences that give kids a break from screens and build social-emotional capital.

Maryland’s children deserve a summer that is not just a break from school but a bridge to something better. With increased focus, commitment, and resolve, we can make that happen.
